lines.text: Exams? Group chat? Holiday shopping? Nah. I don't get stressed. I'm him.

Yo, it's ya boy Cyto, live from the 6ix… inside your body. And right now your body is lowkey panicking. Today we find out why, what it's doing to you, plus one study that had me going "bro, what." And the cheat codes to shut this alarm off before the break. Not medical advice, just your boy and some science.
Incident two. Secret Santa group chat. Forty-three members. Twenty dollar limit.
Incident three. The mall. Packed like Line 1 at rush hour.
Incident four. Your auntie asked what you're doing with your life.

Welcome to the pickup game nobody asked for! Your brain saw stress and hit the alarm. The signal runs down to your adrenal glands, these little condos sitting right on top of your kidneys. And they start pumping out stress hormones, like adrenaline and cortisol.
Adrenaline checks in! Heart rate going UP!
And sugar gets dumped into the blood for quick energy. Mito catches it in the paint…
Your whole body is getting ready to fight or run. This system was built for running from a bear.
There's no bear. It's a group chat.
And every time the phone buzzes, the alarm checks back in. Again. And again.
Bro, who keeps subbing him in?!
Now, a little stress? Normal. Useful, even. But days and days of it? That's where it gets weird.

Cortisol is supposed to tell your immune system "aight, calm down." But researchers at Carnegie Mellon found that when stress drags on, immune cells can stop listening. So inflammation doesn't shut off properly.
See? Security's distracted. And you know who loves a distracted officer?
Scientists took almost four hundred volunteers. Measured how stressed they were. Then they dripped cold viruses into their noses.
Then they waited. Watched who got sick.
Low stress. About seventy-four percent infected. High stress. About ninety.
Actual colds. Twenty-seven percent… up to forty-seven.
So you know how you finally get a break and then you get sick right away? Yeah. Stress might be the reason.
Alarm's still going. Somebody keeps pulling it.

Real quick, serious. Some studies have even found more heart attacks around Christmas and New Year's. Not every study, to be fair. But scientists think stress, giant meals, salt, alcohol, and people waiting too long to get help could all play a part.
So if somebody has chest pain over the holidays, don't wait it out. Call nine one one.
Aight. I made this mess, I'm fixing it. Cheat codes.

Cheat code one: slow your breathing. A randomized trial had people practise slow breathing for twelve weeks, and their anxiety scores dropped. Plot twist: making the exhale longer than the inhale didn't really matter. The slow part did. So, in through the nose… and slow out.

Cheat code two: pick your side quest. Another trial compared exercise, meditation, and slow-breathing training for five weeks. All three lowered stress about the same. So pick whatever you'll actually do.
It's brick outside, so bundle up. Skate at Nathan Phillips Square under the lights, walk the Distillery Winter Village, it's free before four p.m., or just walk the block with your headphones in.
Cheat code three: mute the group chat for a bit. Say no to one thing. Protect your sleep, fam.
Yo… mans are marved. Is that… holiday food?
Mito, chill. That's a Christmas problem.
Comment what's stressing you out the most this December, I read them all. Like, subscribe, sources on screen and in the description. Not medical advice. December's a lot, fam… breathe.
